title: Doubling time and half-life
objectives: Compute a doubling time or half-life from a continuous rate, $T = \tfrac{\ln 2}{k}$
Check the rule of 72 against the exact yearly formula
Recognise that exponential decay halves repeatedly and never reaches zero

screens.title: Doubling time and half-life
screens.prose: How long until money doubles, or a position halves? One logarithm, $\ln 2$, answers both.
£1,000.00 grows continuously at 7% a year. The curve shows its value in thousands of pounds. Drag P along it.
screens.question: Drag P to the moment the money has doubled to £2,000.00.

hints.text: Follow the curve until it meets the dashed line at 2.
The curve crosses the dashed line just before 10 years.
Put P at about 9.9 years, where the caption reads about £2,000.00.

feedback.correct: The money doubles after about 9.9 years.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Stop P where the curve meets the dashed line.

byKey.P: P is not on the £2,000.00 line yet. Move it until the caption reads close to £2,000.00.

explain.text: The curve reaches £2,000.00 at about 9.9 years. Check: $e^{0.07 \times 9.9} = e^{0.693} = 2.00$. Notice the power, 0.693.

screens.prose: Slide the rate $k$. The point marks the moment the money doubles. Try four or five different rates.

derive.caption: At {{(100*k).toFixed(1)}}% the money doubles after {{(log(2)/k).toFixed(2)}} years

screens.question: Multiply the rate, as a percentage, by the doubling time. What do you get?

options.why: Check one: at 4% the time is 17.33 years, and $4 \times 17.33 = 69.3$. The 72 is a rounded rule for yearly payments.

options.text: A bigger number at higher rates
options.why: Try 2% and 12%: $2 \times 34.66 = 69.3$ and $12 \times 5.776 = 69.3$. The product holds still.
You may be thinking of simple interest, which doubles when rate × years = 100. Compounding gets there sooner.

hints.text: At 5%, the caption gives 13.86 years. What is $5 \times 13.86$?

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Work out the product at two different rates.

explain.text: At 4% you got 17.33 years and at 10% you got 6.93: each product is 69.3. Doubling the rate halves the time. We will see where 69.3 comes from next.

canvas.caption: At 10.0% the money doubles after 6.93 years

screens.prose: The time to double is the **doubling time**, $T$. At rate $k$ it solves $e^{kT} = 2$. Taking ln of both sides gives $kT = \ln 2 = 0.6931$.
screens.question: What is the doubling time at a continuous rate of 5% a year, in years to two decimal places?

hints.text: Divide $\ln 2$ by the rate.
Use $k = 0.05$, not 5.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Solve $e^{0.05T} = 2$ with ln.

byKey.simple: That is how long simple interest takes: 5% of the start, 20 times. Compounding doubles sooner.
byKey.72: That is the rule of 72, an estimate for yearly payments. Continuous compounding uses $\ln 2 = 0.6931$.
byKey.pct: You divided by 5 instead of 0.05. The rate goes in as a decimal.

explain.text: $e^{0.05T} = 2$ gives $0.05T = \ln 2$, so $T = 13.86$ years. That is the 69.3 from the explore: $69.3 \div 5 = 13.86$.

screens.prose: Decay runs the same way. Inflation of 3% a year, continuously, shrinks the real value of £1,000.00 of cash to $1000e^{-0.03t}$.

state.caption: £1,000.00 of cash losing 3% a year to inflation, continuously

screens.question: How many years until the cash buys only half as much? Give two decimal places.

hints.text: The curve meets the dashed £500.00 line a little past 20 years.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Take ln of both sides of $e^{-0.03t} = \tfrac{1}{2}$.

byKey.linear: You took 3% of the original £1,000.00 off every year. Each year loses 3% of a smaller amount, so halving takes longer.
byKey.72: That is $72 \div 3$, the yearly rule of thumb. The continuous answer uses 69.3.

explain.text: $\ln \tfrac{1}{2} = -\ln 2$, so the minus signs cancel and $t = \tfrac{\ln 2}{0.03} = 23.10$ years. This is the **half-life**. It has the same formula as the doubling time.

screens.prose: Paid once a year at rate $r$, money doubles when $(1 + r)^T = 2$, so $T = \tfrac{\ln 2}{\ln(1 + r)}$. The rule of 72 estimates $T$ as $72 \div$ the rate in percent.

state.caption: Above 0 the rule is too long; below 0 it is too short

screens.question: Find the exact doubling times, to two decimal places.

hints.text: Divide $\ln 2 = 0.6931$ by $\ln(1 + r)$ for each rate.
The chart shows how far the rule is off at each rate.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Use $T = \tfrac{\ln 2}{\ln(1 + r)}$ with $r$ as a decimal.

byKey.r1c2: Check the 8% row: divide by $\ln 1.08 = 0.0770$, not by 0.08.
byKey.r2c2: Check the 24% row: $\ln 1.24 = 0.2151$. Dividing by 0.24 instead gives 2.89.

explain.text: The rule is almost exact near 8%, a year too long at 2%, and too short at 24%. The error curve crosses zero near 8%. That is why traders trust the rule of 72 only for moderate rates.

screens.prose: A fund's value decays continuously with a half-life of 5 years: after 5 years half of it is left.
screens.question: What fraction of the value is left after 10 years?

options.why: You treated the decay as a straight line: half gone in 5 years, so all gone in 10. Each 5 years removes half of what is left.
You read the half-life as a floor. The value keeps shrinking; the next 5 years halve it again.

hints.text: After 5 years half is left. What happens to that half over the next 5 years?
Follow the curve to 10 years.
Two half-lives: $\tfrac{1}{2} \times \tfrac{1}{2} = \tfrac{1}{4}$.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Halve, then halve again.

byKey.zero: You treated the half-life as half the lifetime. Exponential decay never reaches zero; each half-life halves what remains.

explain.text: Each 5 years multiplies the value by $\tfrac{1}{2}$, so 10 years multiply it by $\tfrac{1}{4}$. The curve never touches zero. After 20 years $\tfrac{1}{16}$ is still left.

screens.prose: You solved $e^{kT} = 2$ and $e^{-kT} = \tfrac{1}{2}$ the same way. Growth at rate $k$ doubles, and decay at rate $k$ halves, in $$T = \frac{\ln 2}{k} \approx \frac{69.3}{\text{rate in }\%}.$$ Paid yearly, $T = \tfrac{\ln 2}{\ln(1 + r)}$, which the rule of 72 approximates.
screens.question: A holding grows at a continuous 3.5% a year. About how long does it take to double?

options.why: That is $100 \div 3.5$, the simple-interest time. Compounding doubles sooner.
That is $72 \div 3.5$, the yearly rule. For continuous growth use 69.3.

hints.text: Divide 69.3 by 3.5.

explain.text: $T = \tfrac{\ln 2}{0.035} = 19.80$ years. The same 19.80 years would halve something decaying at 3.5%.

screens.prose: Where does $\tfrac{\ln 2}{k}$ come from? Derive it from the meaning of doubling.
screens.question: Put the steps in order.

lines.text: $Pe^{kT} = 2P$: after time $T$ the amount is twice the start
$kT = \ln 2$: take ln of both sides, since ln undoes $e$

hints.text: Start from what doubling means for the amount.
Write the doubling, cancel $P$, take ln, then divide by $k$.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Each line rewrites the one above it.

byKey.d3: Before taking ln, the $e$-power must be alone, so divide by $P$ first.
byKey.d2: Start from the meaning of doubling, $Pe^{kT} = 2P$.

explain.text: The start amount $P$ cancels, so the doubling time does not depend on how much you have. Taking ln leaves $kT = \ln 2$. Every doubling takes the same $T$.

screens.prose: A desk unwinds a £40,000,000.00 position by selling continuously. After $t$ trading days the holding is $40e^{-0.15t}$ million pounds.
screens.question: After how many trading days is half the position left? Give two decimal places.

hints.text: The curve meets the £20 million line just under 5 days.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. The half-life is $\tfrac{\ln 2}{k}$.

byKey.linear: You sold 15% of the original each day. The desk sells at a continuous rate on what is left, so halving takes longer.
byKey.72: That is $72 \div 15$. For continuous decay use $\ln 2$, which gives 69.3.

explain.text: The half-life is $\tfrac{\ln 2}{0.15} = 4.62$ trading days. After 9.24 days a quarter, £10,000,000.00, is still held. Execution desks quote unwind speed this way.

ideas: Solving $e^{kT} = 2$ with ln gives the doubling time $T = \tfrac{\ln 2}{k}$, whatever the starting amount.
Decay at rate $k$ halves in the same time; each half-life halves what is left.
Paid yearly, $T = \tfrac{\ln 2}{\ln(1 + r)}$; the rule of 72 is close near 8%.

formula.name: Doubling time and half-life
formula.note: For a rate paid once a year, $T = \dfrac{\ln 2}{\ln(1 + r)}$.

summary.trap: Two half-lives leave a quarter, not nothing. Exponential decay never reaches zero.

quiz.prose: Money grows at a continuous 10% a year.
quiz.question: What is its doubling time, in years to two decimal places?

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Divide $\ln 2$ by the rate as a decimal.

byKey.72: That is the rule of 72. Continuous growth gives $\tfrac{\ln 2}{0.1} = 6.93$.
byKey.simple: That is the simple-interest time. Compounding doubles sooner.

quiz.prose: A trading signal's strength decays with a half-life of 3 days.
quiz.question: What fraction of its strength is left after 9 days?

options.why: You let it fall in a straight line. Each 3 days halves what is left, so it never reaches zero.
You divided 3 by 9. Count half-lives instead: 9 days is three of them.
You put $2 \times 3$ underneath. Three halvings multiply: $(\tfrac{1}{2})^3 = \tfrac{1}{8}$.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Count the half-lives in 9 days.

explain.text: 9 days is three half-lives. $\tfrac{1}{2} \times \tfrac{1}{2} \times \tfrac{1}{2} = \tfrac{1}{8}$ of the strength is left.

quiz.prose: An investment doubles in 12 years with continuous compounding.
quiz.question: What is its continuous rate, as a percentage to two decimal places?

byKey.72: That is $72 \div 12$, the yearly rule. Continuous compounding uses $\ln 2$.
byKey.simple: That is $100 \div 12$, the simple-interest rate. Compounding needs less.

explain.text: $k = \tfrac{\ln 2}{T} = \tfrac{0.6931}{12} = 0.0578$. A continuous 5.78% doubles money in 12 years.

quiz.prose: A savings account pays 1% once a year. The rule of 72 says it doubles in 72 years.
quiz.question: What is the exact doubling time, in years to two decimal places?

byKey.72: That is the rule's estimate. At 1% it runs more than 2 years long.
byKey.cont: That is the continuous answer, $\tfrac{\ln 2}{0.01}$. Paid once a year, divide by $\ln 1.01 = 0.00995$.

explain.text: $\ln 1.01 = 0.00995$, so $T = \tfrac{0.6931}{0.00995} = 69.66$ years. The rule of 72 overstates it by 2.34 years at this low rate.
